studies.headline: Tell shoppers they're building a collection, not just buying a thing
studies.the_study: Across seven preregistered experiments plus one supplemental study (N=3,306), researchers tested what happens when a purchase is framed as adding to the consumer's own collection rather than as a one-off buy. Framing acquisition as "collecting" made the shopping process itself more enjoyable and raised how desirable the sought product seemed, because attention shifted from securing a standalone item to advancing a collection. The effect was strongest when consumers actively searched, when the find genuinely advanced the collection, and when the collection tied to an identity they valued — and it weakened or reversed otherwise.
studies.why_it_matters: Retailers have spent a decade stripping friction out of search; this suggests the opposite move — making search feel like a curatorial quest — can increase willingness to buy and make the process itself a source of value.
studies.story_angle_primary: A cheap copy and merchandising test: reframe category pages, loyalty tiers, or recommendation modules around "your collection" rather than "items you may like," and watch whether desirability and conversion move. But note the boundary conditions — frictionless one-click flows and generic product sets may neutralize or invert the effect, so test before rolling out.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It explains why sneaker drops, trading cards, makeup shades and vinyl crates hook people so effectively: the pleasure is in the hunt and the sense of a set being completed, not in the object. Knowing the trick is being deployed on you is a useful defense at checkout.
studies.caveats: All studies are experiments, largely with online participants; product desirability and acquisition experience are measured responses rather than observed long-run purchases, and the effect depends on identity-relevant collections.
studies.paper_title: EXPRESS: The Collecting Mindset: Viewing Purchasing as Collecting Enhances Acquisition Experience and Product Desirability

studies.headline: Launching a green product line lifted the parent brand — but only for firms with clean reputations
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a staggered event study around a major laundry detergent brand's first sustainable product line launch, then extended the analysis to subsequent sustainable new product introductions across 15 leading brands sold in 12 retail chains. Sustainable launches measurably increased parent-brand equity, acting as a credible product-based signal of environmental responsibility. The lift was conditional: it was stronger when the parent firm already had an ethical reputation and when the retail chain carried a higher share of sustainable products.
studies.why_it_matters: It puts a brand-equity number on sustainability launches beyond the sales of the green item itself — and shows the halo is borrowed against existing credibility rather than created from nothing.
studies.story_angle_primary: Treat a sustainable line extension as a brand investment, not just an SKU decision, and model the parent-brand return — but audit your own ethical track record first, since the evidence suggests firms with weak reputations get little signaling benefit. Retail placement matters too: the same product appears to signal more in chains already known for sustainable assortments.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Shoppers may be reading more into a green product than its packaging claims: a single eco line can shift how the whole brand is perceived, which is exactly why greenwashing accusations sting so much.
studies.caveats: Observational market data rather than a randomized test; anchored in one category (laundry detergent) for the main event study and a limited set of brands and chains; results reflect one retail market and may not generalize across categories.
studies.journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
studies.paper_title: Can green innovations enhance competitive advantage?

studies.headline: In live shopping, the host's mood moves sales — and the sidekick may be costing you money
studies.the_study: Analyzing minute-by-minute data from 40 Taobao live streaming sessions (4,671 minutes total), researchers used sentiment analysis to quantify streamers' and viewers' emotional expression, then modeled the dynamics with a panel vector autoregression. Emotion flowed one way: streamer emotion was closely linked to viewer interaction and purchases, while viewer-to-viewer emotional contagion was not statistically supported. Viewer emotion was tied to new follower growth, and more frequent intervention by the on-screen assistant raised interaction frequency but was negatively associated with product sales.
studies.why_it_matters: Live commerce teams optimize for engagement metrics; this suggests chat activity and sales can pull in opposite directions, and that the host's emotional performance is the main lever on revenue.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit whether your live-stream assistant's interjections are buying chatter at the expense of conversion, and consider coaching and scheduling hosts around sustained emotional energy rather than chasing comment volume. The data are observational and from a single platform, so treat it as a hypothesis to A/B test in your own streams.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The enthusiasm in a live shopping stream is not just ambiance — the host's excitement is statistically connected to what viewers buy in the following minutes, a useful thing to notice before you tap "add to cart."
studies.caveats: Observational panel data from 40 sessions on one platform (Taobao) in one market; associations and impulse responses, not randomized causal evidence; sentiment is inferred algorithmically from text and speech.
studies.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
studies.paper_title: Emotional interaction and conversion value in live streaming E-commerce

studies.headline: When the shock hit, paid search carried e-commerce revenue — and Facebook ads brought visitors who didn't buy
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed a 71-week Google Analytics panel covering 24 online retailers, comparing how site entry channels, visitor status and transaction value related to revenue before and during the COVID-19 lockdown disruption. Direct traffic and repeat visitors were consistently the strongest revenue correlates in both periods, while paid search became a notably stronger revenue pathway during the disruption. Facebook ads were associated with first-time visitor volume but little immediate revenue, and lagged models showed paid search spending today predicted later organic search and direct visits.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives marketers real platform-level evidence that paid search has a delayed halo on "free" channels, and that social-driven first-time traffic should not be judged on same-session revenue.
studies.story_angle_primary: Revisit attribution windows: if paid search reliably precedes later organic and direct arrivals, last-click models will systematically understate it — and cutting search spend in a downturn may quietly erode the direct traffic you rely on. Also reconsider the KPI you set for social ads, which here delivered audience rather than immediate sales.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Your own shopping path explains the finding: people often discover a retailer via an ad or search, then come back later by typing the name directly — which is why the channel that got credit for your purchase is rarely the one that actually found you.
studies.caveats: Observational panel of 24 retailers only, with associations rather than causal estimates; the disruption period is a unique exogenous shock that may not generalize to normal conditions or to other markets and platforms.
studies.paper_title: Impacts on E-Commerce Revenue Before and During an Exogenous Shock: Site Entry Channels, Visitor Status, and Transaction Value

studies.headline: A little blue check moved eyeballs — and choices — in a risky online marketplace
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a controlled eye-tracking experiment with 60 participants who each browsed 10 NFT listings, with five listings randomly assigned a platform-issued verification badge, then picked three for a hypothetical purchase. Badged item cards drew a fixation in 83.3% of observations versus 35.7% for unbadged cards, were looked at roughly 1.47 seconds sooner, and were chosen 42.3% of the time versus 17.7% for unbadged listings. The effect was concentrated among participants who said afterward they had clearly noticed the badge, suggesting the signal only works once it captures attention.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives process-level evidence that trust badges on marketplace listings work less as a reasoned credibility argument and more as an attention magnet that gets a listing into the consideration set at all.
studies.story_angle_primary: For platform and marketplace teams: this is a case for A/B testing badge placement, size and contrast — not just whether to have a verification program, but whether shoppers actually see it. The study suggests the conversion lift is gated on noticing, so a badge buried in a card layout may be doing nothing. Treat this as a controlled-lab signal of what can happen, not a guaranteed lift on live traffic.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Shoppers may want to ask what a verification badge actually certifies. In this study a randomly assigned badge — carrying no real quality information — more than doubled selection rates, a reminder that a visual trust cue can steer choice before you've consciously evaluated the item.
studies.caveats: Small sample (60 participants); hypothetical selections rather than real purchases; a single, unusual category (NFT listings) in a controlled interface; gaze was measured for the whole item card, not the badge icon itself; badge 'noticing' was self-reported after the task, not manipulated.
studies.paper_title: Visual trust signals in digital financial marketplaces: eye-tracking evidence from verification badges

studies.headline: Loyalty programs don't fail on rewards alone — trust and commitment have to show up too
studies.the_study: Two surveys of Australian supermarket shoppers (N=250 to validate the engagement measure, N=820 to test the model) examined what makes customers actually engage with loyalty programs, using both PLS-SEM and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis. Customers' own inclination and capacity to engage — including their habits of searching for deals over time and across stores — predicted loyalty program engagement, which in turn predicted engagement with the retailer and both attitudinal and behavioral loyalty. The configurational analysis found that perceived benefits, trust and commitment together form the key recipe: their joint presence drives engagement, and their joint absence blocks it.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests loyalty program performance is not simply a function of how generous the rewards are, but of whether a particular customer is disposed to engage at all — pointing toward segmenting programs by engagement propensity rather than treating all members alike.
studies.story_angle_primary: For retail CRM and loyalty leads: the practical question is whether your program is over-indexed on benefit richness while underinvesting in trust signals (data use, reward transparency, reliability of redemption). Worth testing whether segmenting members by engagement disposition — deal-seekers versus passive enrollees — changes program ROI more than another points tweak.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A useful consumer-side read: the people who get the most out of supermarket loyalty programs are those already inclined to hunt for deals across stores and over time. If you're a passive member, the program is likely delivering far less value to you than to the engaged shopper next to you in line.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional surveys, so causal direction cannot be established; self-reported loyalty and engagement rather than observed purchase data; single country (Australia) and single sector (supermarkets).
studies.paper_title: Customers’ disposition towards loyalty program engagement

studies.headline: AI review summaries didn't silence shoppers — they wrote more reviews, and better ones
studies.the_study: Researchers studied an e-commerce platform's rollout of AI-generated summaries (AIGS) of customer reviews, comparing review behavior before and after the feature appeared, and added a controlled lab experiment that measured the psychological mechanism. Contrary to the intuition that AI-written content crowds out user-generated content, review volume rose after AIGS was introduced, with the lab study showing the effect was mediated by a heightened sense of "collective efficacy" — the feeling that one's individual review feeds a shared body of product knowledge. The lift was strongest for products that were already well-reviewed and for polarizing products. Content analysis showed post-AIGS reviews covered fewer attributes the summary already mentioned, raised more attributes it had missed, and elaborated rather than restated.
studies.why_it_matters: Retailers worried that generative-AI summaries would cannibalize the user reviews they depend on now have evidence of the opposite — summaries can act as a recruitment device for more, and more informative, contributions.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're piloting AI review summaries, instrument the downstream effect on review volume and content quality, not just on conversion or time-on-page; the mechanism here suggests the framing of the summary (as a collective product of shoppers' contributions) may be what drives the lift, which is a testable design variable.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The AI summary at the top of a product page may be quietly changing what shoppers write: people stop repeating the obvious and start filling the gaps, which means reviews posted after a summary exists may be more useful to read than the ones above them.
studies.caveats: Observational data from a single e-commerce platform with a before/after design; the mediation evidence comes from a separate controlled lab experiment; effects on well-reviewed and polarizing products may not generalize to thin catalogs; short post-introduction horizon.
studies.paper_title: Navigating the Sea of Reviews: Unveiling the Effects of Introducing AI-Generated Summaries in E-Commerce

studies.headline: On B2B platforms, a strong online reputation and a strong trade-show presence cancel each other out
studies.the_study: Using 30 months of operational data from sellers on a major Chinese B2B platform, researchers tested whether online reputation scores and participation in offline events reinforce each other. Both were independently associated with better seller performance, and online reputation mattered more on average — but their interaction was negative: the payoff from each weakened as the other grew stronger. The authors interpret both as credibility cues that substitute for one another once a buyer already has a strong signal.
studies.why_it_matters: It challenges the default omnichannel assumption that online and offline investments compound, and suggests B2B sellers with already-excellent ratings may be over-spending on event budgets.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit whether your offline event spend is concentrated on sellers or business units that already have top-tier online ratings — this analysis implies the marginal return there is lowest, and the budget may do more work behind weakly rated or newly listed offerings.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Buyers appear to stop collecting evidence once one credibility signal is convincing enough — a useful reminder of how quickly people settle on "good enough" proof before committing.
studies.caveats: Observational platform data from a single Chinese B2B marketplace; the paper carefully describes associations rather than causal effects; selection into offline events is not randomized.
studies.paper_title: Cross-Channel effects of online reputation and offline event participation in B2B Platforms: Synergy or Attenuation?

studies.headline: Fun-seeking shoppers forgive influencers who stray off-topic; practical shoppers don't
studies.the_study: Across five experiments, researchers treated social media influencers as "person brands" and tested how consumers react when an influencer recommends something outside their usual domain. Purchase motivation moderated the effect: hedonic, fun-driven shoppers were relatively tolerant of low-relevance recommendations, while functionally motivated shoppers punished them — and for the functional group, the damage ran through perceived influencer authenticity. When the product was far outside the influencer's lane, hedonic consumers responded better to warm influencers than to competent-seeming ones.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives brands a concrete rule for matching influencer partnerships to category and shopping mindset, rather than assuming reach and follower fit are enough.
studies.story_angle_primary: Test whether your category is bought hedonically or functionally before buying off-domain influencer reach: for utilitarian products the evidence points to tight domain fit and authenticity signals, while for indulgence categories warmth may beat expertise even on a stretch recommendation.
studies.story_angle_secondary: That nagging sense that a favorite creator has "sold out" when they post about something unrelated appears to depend on why you're watching — people shopping for a solution judge harshly, people shopping for fun largely shrug.
studies.caveats: Five experiments, likely with online panel participants and hypothetical products; measures are purchase intentions rather than observed purchases; sample details and country not specified in the abstract.
studies.paper_title: How consumers respond to social media influencers’ cross-domain recommendations?——A person brand perspective

studies.headline: Three in four Vietnamese grocery shoppers will pay for home delivery — but they're exquisitely sensitive to the fee
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a discrete choice experiment with 438 grocery shoppers in Vietnam's Mekong Delta, estimating willingness to pay for last-mile delivery attributes using a generalized multinomial logit model in willingness-to-pay space that allows for both taste and scale heterogeneity. About 75% of consumers showed positive willingness to pay for home delivery, but demand was highly sensitive to shipping fees, and willingness to pay for each attribute varied widely across individuals, driven by both demographics and order value as well as unobserved taste differences.
studies.why_it_matters: It's rare WTP evidence for e-grocery delivery in a developing market, and it argues against flat, one-size-fits-all shipping fees in favor of segmented or order-value-conditioned delivery options.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you operate e-grocery in an emerging market, treat the delivery fee as a segmentation lever rather than a fixed cost pass-through — the heterogeneity here suggests menu-based options (speed, window, price tiers) tied to order value could capture more demand than a single flat fee.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Most shoppers do value having groceries brought to the door — but the price at which that value evaporates is lower and more variable than retailers tend to assume, which is why the delivery fee is so often the thing that kills a cart.
studies.caveats: Hypothetical choice scenarios, not observed purchases; a single region of one country; modest sample (N=438) for the number of segments explored; stated preferences may overstate real willingness to pay.
studies.paper_title: Willingness to pay for last-mile delivery service: the case of omnichannel grocery retailing in the Mekong Delta, Vietnam

studies.headline: The myth of the "bad returner": eight years of Nordic fashion data says returns don't drive future spending — or kill profit
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed archival data from a Nordic fashion e-tailer covering 2015–2022: 260,698 orders from 110,772 customers. Using Bernoulli modeling, difference-in-differences with matched control customers, and a profitability threshold analysis, they found that nearly every long-tenured customer eventually becomes a "returner" simply through exposure, and that making a return had no detectable causal effect on how much a customer bought afterward (DiD = −0.0031, p = 0.62). Declines in spending showed up equally among matched non-returners, pointing to normal customer lifecycle decay rather than anything caused by the return itself. Returners reached profit parity with non-returners once reverse-logistics costs fell below a calculable recovery threshold.
studies.why_it_matters: Retailers routinely segment, flag, and even ban "serial returners," but this evidence suggests returner status is mostly a function of how long someone has shopped with you — and the real profit lever is the cost of processing returns, not the customer's behavior.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit whether your returns policy and customer-scoring models are punishing a customer type that may not exist. The actionable question shifts from "who returns too much?" to "what does a return cost us to process, and where is our break-even threshold?" — a single-retailer finding worth replicating against your own order history before rewriting policy.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If you've worried that sending items back marks you as a problem customer, the data from one large retailer suggests returning is close to universal among regular shoppers — and returners spent no less afterward than anyone else.
studies.caveats: Single retailer, single category (fashion) and a single region (Nordic market); archival and observational, so matched-control DiD mitigates but does not eliminate selection effects; the profitability threshold depends on that firm's specific reverse-logistics cost structure.
studies.journal: The International Review of Retail Distribution and Consumer Research
studies.paper_title: Exploring the returner profitability paradox: exposure mechanisms, lifecycle transitions, and operational cost-recovery thresholds

studies.headline: Simple beats smart: basic rule-based chatbots outperformed LLM bots on retail service logs
studies.the_study: A two-part mixed-methods study used real chatbot logs rather than lab tests. Study 1 covered 108,566 sessions across nine rule-based chatbots in four industries in Portugal and Brazil during 2023, finding that efficiency — how little effort it took to resolve a query — was strongly associated with customers returning to use the bot (β = .92, p = .004), while effectiveness showed no independent association. Study 2 combined six interviews with Portuguese retail managers and descriptive log data from three rule-based and two LLM retail chatbots (11,320 sessions, 50,321 interactions in 2024), and found the rule-based deployments recorded higher efficiency and effectiveness rates than the LLM systems.
studies.why_it_matters: As retailers rush to replace scripted bots with generative AI, operational logs from live deployments suggest the newer technology did not automatically deliver better service outcomes — and that minimizing customer effort mattered more for repeat use than getting the answer perfectly right.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before swapping a working rule-based bot for an LLM, instrument both and compare on effort-per-resolution, not on demo impressiveness. The result also hints at a design principle worth A/B testing: optimizing for fewer turns and faster resolution may buy more repeat usage than optimizing for conversational richness.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It helps explain a common frustration: a chatty AI assistant that takes five exchanges to do what a menu of buttons did in one can feel worse, even when it's technically more capable.
studies.caveats: Observational and correlational — no causal claims possible; very small samples at the chatbot level (nine bots in Study 1, five in Study 2) and Study 2 did not compare revisit rates between architectures at all; limited to Portugal and Brazil; LLM deployments were early-generation and may improve.
studies.journal: The International Review of Retail Distribution and Consumer Research
studies.paper_title: Simplicity over sophistication? Rule-based chatbots lead to higher return rates than LLMs in retail

studies.headline: Why India's lowest-income shoppers stay loyal to one store — and it isn't trust
studies.the_study: Researchers studied retail and brand choice among base-of-the-pyramid consumers in semi-urban West Bengal, India, combining 48 grounded-theory interviews to build measures with a survey of 342 low-income consumers analyzed via PLS-SEM. Bounded rationality (limited information and literacy) and lock-in — credit ties, proximity, dependence on a single shopkeeper — significantly drove constrained store selection, which in turn constrained which brands people could buy. Perceived opportunism, meaning the suspicion that retailers exploit them, was present but did not meaningfully shape either constraint.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that for subsistence consumers, brand choice is effectively decided at the store level before a brand ever competes: win the shopkeeper and the credit relationship, and you win the basket.
studies.story_angle_primary: For companies targeting emerging-market mass segments, this points to distribution and retailer relationships — not advertising — as the binding constraint on brand access, and raises an uncomfortable test: is your growth in these markets coming from preference or from shoppers having nowhere else to go?
studies.story_angle_secondary: A reminder that "consumer choice" is partly a privilege of mobility and information; when a neighborhood shop extends you credit, your shopping list is shaped by that relationship long before any brand message reaches you.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey, so no causal inference; self-reported attitudes rather than observed purchases; confined to semi-urban West Bengal and may not generalize to other Indian regions or emerging markets; retailer perspectives not captured; constructs are newly developed and not yet externally validated.
studies.paper_title: Constrained Choices: Exploring Retail and Brand Selection Among Base of the Pyramid Consumers

studies.headline: Giving your shopping assistant a face: when human-looking AI avatars actually lift engagement
studies.the_study: Two studies tested whether making AI service avatars look more human changes how shoppers respond. Study 1 was a between-subjects experiment manipulating bundled visual anthropomorphism (more versus less human-looking avatar); Study 2 was a three-wave survey of online shoppers recalling real AI-avatar service encounters, analyzed with PROCESS mediation and moderation using 5,000 bootstrap resamples. More human-looking avatars raised engagement intention, and emotional connection explained part — but only part — of the effect. Perceived authenticity strengthened the link from anthropomorphism to emotional connection, while technological familiarity strengthened the link from emotional connection to engagement.
studies.why_it_matters: Retailers are rapidly deploying avatar-fronted AI assistants on the assumption that a friendlier face builds rapport; this work suggests the lift is real but modest, and depends on whether users read the avatar as authentic and are already comfortable with the technology.
studies.story_angle_primary: Treat avatar design as a testable variable, not a default: run holdout tests comparing a human-looking avatar against a plain text or icon-based assistant, and segment results by how tech-fluent your customer base is. The paper's own finding that emotional connection carries only part of the effect is a warning against over-investing in warmth cues at the expense of competence, speed and accuracy.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A shopping bot with eyes and a name is designed to trigger the same social instincts you use with people — and this research suggests it partly works, especially if the persona feels authentic rather than cloying.
studies.caveats: Study 2 is a self-reported survey of recalled encounters and cannot establish causation; Study 1 measures engagement intentions rather than purchases; sample size and country for both studies are not specified in the abstract; effects on emotional connection were described as comparatively modest.
studies.journal: Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing
studies.paper_title: When and how anthropomorphic AI avatars relate to user engagement intentions: roles of emotional connection, perceived authenticity and technological familiarity

studies.headline: Scams are now a marketing problem: researchers reframe AI fraud as 'malicious persuasion'
studies.the_study: This conceptual article in the Journal of Interactive Marketing treats online scams as AI-driven malicious persuasion attempts, arguing that generative AI changes fraud on three dimensions at once: simplicity of creation, sophistication of execution and scale of distribution. Drawing on persuasion knowledge theory and a dynamic view of consumer vulnerability, the authors argue vulnerability is both a cause of being scammed and a consequence of it — victimization deepens susceptibility. They propose consumer empowerment (recognizing and resisting attacks, reporting victimization, and recovering over time) as a necessary complement to regulation and platform self-regulation.
studies.why_it_matters: Fraud erodes trust in the same digital channels legitimate retailers depend on, and this framing makes scam resilience a shared commercial responsibility rather than only a policing issue.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit how closely your own persuasion tactics — urgency countdowns, scarcity claims, lookalike checkout flows — resemble the patterns consumers are being trained to distrust, and consider whether clear authentication and anti-impersonation messaging is becoming a brand asset rather than a compliance cost.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The research reframes being scammed as something that happens to people in a weakened moment rather than to gullible people, and argues that victims spiral: being defrauded once makes the next attempt more likely to land.
studies.caveats: This is a conceptual and agenda-setting paper, not new empirical evidence; the interventions it proposes have not been tested here.
studies.paper_title: EXPRESS: The AI-Driven Scam Economy: Persuasion Knowledge, Consumer Vulnerability, and Empowerment

studies.headline: The original purpose-driven brand: what Gandhi's homespun cloth campaign got right — and where it hit a wall
studies.the_study: A qualitative historical case study reanalyzes khadi, the indigenous hand-spun cloth of India's Swadeshi and Non-Cooperation movements, as an early campaign of ethnocentric countermarketing. The author synthesizes archival visual material, period print advertisements and historical economic data through the lenses of social identity theory and consumer ethnocentrism. The conclusion: khadi won not by being a better product but by rewriting the evaluation criteria so that symbolic identity value outweighed clear functional shortcomings — yet price gaps, class divides and technological dependence kept it from displacing colonial supply chains.
studies.why_it_matters: It is a historical stress test of purpose-driven branding, showing both that meaning can override product inferiority and that symbolic positioning collapses without scalable cost and supply infrastructure behind it.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your brand is asking customers to accept a functional trade-off for a values-based reason, treat the supply chain as the binding constraint: the case suggests identity-led demand can be created faster than the operations needed to serve it affordably at scale.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A century before boycotts and buycotts went viral online, shoppers were already using what they bought to signal who they were — and the same economics applied: the ethical choice cost more, which limited who could make it.
studies.caveats: Interpretive historical case study, not a controlled or quantitative design; the author notes reliance on compiled historical literature and published archival media rather than raw trade ledgers; single country and single movement, so generalization to modern brands is inferential.
studies.journal: Journal of Historical Research in Marketing
studies.paper_title: A case study on khadi: ethnocentric countermarketing and social identity in colonial resistance

fact_check.headline: Tell shoppers they're building a collection, not just buying a thing
fact_check.notes: Design, N and boundary conditions all match the abstract. Two small slips: 'willingness to buy' substitutes for the measured outcome (product desirability), and the caveat asserts participant sourcing the abstract never states.

issues.label: Outcome restated as willingness to buy
issues.as_written: can increase willingness to buy and make the process itself a source of value
issues.abstract_says: improves consumers’ acquisition experience and increases product desirability
issues.problem: The measured outcomes are acquisition experience and product desirability; 'willingness to buy' is a different, purchase-proximal construct not reported in the abstract.
issues.suggested_fix: Say the framing 'raised how desirable the product seemed and made the search itself more enjoyable' rather than 'willingness to buy'.

issues.label: Participant pool not specified in abstract
issues.as_written: All studies are experiments, largely with online participants
issues.abstract_says: seven preregistered studies plus one supplemental study (N = 3,306)
issues.problem: The abstract gives no information about where participants were recruited; 'largely with online participants' is unverifiable from abstract only.
issues.suggested_fix: Drop the claim or hedge: 'participant sources are not specified in the abstract.'

fact_check.headline: Launching a green product line lifted the parent brand — but only for firms with clean reputations
fact_check.notes: Event study, 15 brands and 12 chains, and both moderators are reported correctly. The headline's 'only for' and the stated direction of the moderation go slightly beyond an abstract that only says the effect is 'moderated by'.

issues.label: Moderator turned into a necessary condition
issues.as_written: Launching a green product line lifted the parent brand — but only for firms with clean reputations
issues.abstract_says: A complementary analysis of subsequent SNPIs across 15 leading brands in 12 retail chains reveals that this effect is moderated by parent firms' ethical reputation and retail chains' sustainable assortment share.
issues.problem: The abstract reports a moderation, not a condition under which the effect disappears; the main event study shows a positive effect without that qualifier. The direction of the moderation is also not stated in the abstract.
issues.suggested_fix: Rephrase as 'and the size of the lift depended on the firm's ethical reputation and the retailer's sustainable assortment'; note that direction is not specified in the abstract.

issues.label: Directional claim about weak-reputation firms
issues.as_written: audit your own ethical track record first, since the evidence suggests firms with weak reputations get little signaling benefit
issues.abstract_says: this effect is moderated by parent firms' ethical reputation and retail chains' sustainable assortment share
issues.problem: The abstract does not quantify or sign the moderation, so 'little signaling benefit' for weak-reputation firms is unverifiable from abstract only.
issues.suggested_fix: Soften to 'the payoff appears to depend on existing ethical reputation, though the abstract does not report the size or direction of that difference.'

fact_check.headline: In live shopping, the host's mood moves sales — and the sidekick may be costing you money
fact_check.notes: Sample (40 Taobao sessions, 4,671 minutes), PVAR method and all four directional results match the abstract. Headline and 'Why it matters' lean causal where the abstract is strictly associational, though the caveats and both angles correct this.

issues.label: Causal shorthand for associational findings
issues.as_written: the host's emotional performance is the main lever on revenue
issues.abstract_says: streamer emotions are closely associated with viewer interaction and purchase decisions
issues.problem: The study reports associations and impulse responses from observational panel data; 'main lever on revenue' and the headline's 'moves sales' imply demonstrated causation, which the abstract is careful not to claim.
issues.suggested_fix: Use 'the host's emotional energy is the variable most strongly associated with sales' and soften the headline to 'tracks sales'.

fact_check.headline: When the shock hit, paid search carried e-commerce revenue — and Facebook ads brought visitors who didn't buy
fact_check.notes: Panel length, number of retailers, the paid-search and Facebook results are all accurate. Two small embellishments: 'strongest' revenue correlates and 'paid search spending' are not what the abstract states.

issues.label: 'Strongest' not in the abstract
issues.as_written: Direct traffic and repeat visitors were consistently the strongest revenue correlates in both periods
issues.abstract_says: Findings include that direct access and repeat visitors are consistently associated with revenue.
issues.problem: The abstract reports consistency of association, not a ranking of channels by strength.
issues.suggested_fix: Change to 'were consistently associated with revenue in both periods'.

issues.label: Spend substituted for channel
issues.as_written: lagged models showed paid search spending today predicted later organic search and direct visits
issues.abstract_says: Lagged models show paid search is consistently associated with later organic search and direct access.
issues.problem: The abstract refers to the paid search channel, not to spending levels, and frames the result as a lagged association rather than prediction of spend effects.
issues.suggested_fix: Write 'paid search activity was consistently associated with later organic search and direct arrivals'.

fact_check.headline: A little blue check moved eyeballs — and choices — in a risky online marketplace
fact_check.notes: Sample, design, randomization, all three headline percentages and the attention-gating result match the abstract, and the caveats are unusually complete. Only the 1.47-second figure drops the abstract's conditioning clause.

issues.label: Dropped conditioning on the 1.47s estimate
issues.as_written: were looked at roughly 1.47 seconds sooner
issues.abstract_says: Among cards with an observed first fixation, badge assignment was associated with an approximately 1.47-s earlier first fixation.
issues.problem: The estimate applies only to cards that received a first fixation at all; stating it unconditionally slightly overstates its generality.
issues.suggested_fix: Add 'among cards that were fixated at all'.

fact_check.headline: Loyalty programs don't fail on rewards alone — trust and commitment have to show up too
fact_check.notes: Both sample sizes, the Australian supermarket context, the dual PLS-SEM/fsQCA approach and the configurational finding are reported faithfully, and the caveats correctly flag cross-sectional self-report data.

fact_check.headline: AI review summaries didn't silence shoppers — they wrote more reviews, and better ones
fact_check.notes: Direction of effect, the collective-efficacy mediation via a separate lab experiment, both moderators and the content-analysis results all match. Some design and horizon details asserted in the body and caveats are not in the abstract.

issues.label: Design details beyond the abstract
issues.as_written: comparing review behavior before and after the feature appeared
issues.abstract_says: the introduction of AIGS actually leads to an increase in the volume of consumer reviews ... This mechanism is supported by an additional controlled laboratory experiment
issues.problem: The abstract does not describe the empirical design (whether it is a simple before/after comparison, a difference-in-differences, or otherwise), so characterizing it as a before/after design is unverifiable from abstract only.
issues.suggested_fix: Say 'studied the rollout of AI-generated summaries on an e-commerce platform' without specifying the comparison design.

issues.label: Unverifiable time-horizon caveat
issues.problem: The abstract gives no information about the length of the post-introduction period, so this caveat cannot be checked.
issues.suggested_fix: Remove, or note that the observation window is not reported in the abstract.

fact_check.headline: On B2B platforms, a strong online reputation and a strong trade-show presence cancel each other out
fact_check.notes: The 30-month Chinese platform data, the two main effects, the negative interaction and the stronger online-reputation association are all correct; the headline substitutes 'trade shows' for 'offline events' and overstates attenuation as cancellation.

issues.label: Offline events narrowed to trade shows
issues.problem: The abstract refers to offline event participation generally; trade shows are one possible form and are never named.
issues.suggested_fix: Use 'offline event participation' in the headline.

issues.label: 'Cancel each other out' overstates the interaction
issues.abstract_says: their interaction is negative: the conditional association of each mechanism weakens as the other strengthens
issues.problem: A negative interaction means diminishing incremental returns, not mutual cancellation; the body text describes it correctly but the headline exaggerates.
issues.suggested_fix: Headline as 'partly substitute for each other' or 'blunt each other's payoff'.

fact_check.headline: Fun-seeking shoppers forgive influencers who stray off-topic; practical shoppers don't
fact_check.notes: Five experiments, the moderation by purchase motivation, the authenticity mediation limited to functional consumers and the warmth result are all represented. The warmth finding's comparison group is subtly shifted.

issues.label: Warmth comparison shifted
issues.as_written: When the product was far outside the influencer's lane, hedonic consumers responded better to warm influencers than to competent-seeming ones.
issues.abstract_says: when low-relevance products are recommended, hedonic (vs. functional) consumers are inclined to purchase products from warm (vs. competent) influencers
issues.problem: The abstract frames this as a contrast between hedonic and functional consumers in their preference for warm versus competent influencers; the digest reports only the within-hedonic comparison, dropping the functional-consumer half of the contrast.
issues.suggested_fix: Add that the warm-over-competent preference distinguishes hedonic consumers from functional ones.

fact_check.headline: Three in four Vietnamese grocery shoppers will pay for home delivery — but they're exquisitely sensitive to the fee
fact_check.notes: Sample size, Mekong Delta location, the GMNL-in-WTP-space method, the ~75% figure, fee sensitivity and the heterogeneity sources all match. The headline generalizes a single-region sample to Vietnam as a whole.

issues.label: Regional sample generalized to a country
issues.as_written: Three in four Vietnamese grocery shoppers will pay for home delivery
issues.abstract_says: The data was collected from a discrete choice experiment on 438 shoppers in the Mekong Delta, Vietnam. ... Around 75% of consumers have a positive WTP for home delivery.
issues.problem: The 75% figure describes 438 shoppers sampled in one region; the headline presents it as a national statistic, and 'will pay' presents stated choice-experiment preferences as behavior. The caveats correct both, but the headline stands alone.
issues.suggested_fix: Headline as 'Three in four shoppers in Vietnam's Mekong Delta say they'd pay for home delivery'.

fact_check.headline: The myth of the "bad returner": eight years of Nordic fashion data says returns don't drive future spending — or kill profit
fact_check.notes: Sample, period, methods and the DiD statistic all match the abstract; causal language is appropriately hedged and limitations are disclosed.

fact_check.headline: Simple beats smart: basic rule-based chatbots outperformed LLM bots on retail service logs
fact_check.notes: Session counts, countries, years, β = .92 / p = .004 and the Study 2 descriptive comparison all match; the caveat correctly notes Study 2 did not compare revisit rates.

fact_check.headline: Why India's lowest-income shoppers stay loyal to one store — and it isn't trust
fact_check.notes: Core numbers (48 interviews, N=342, PLS-SEM) and the null opportunism result are correct, but the headline reframes constrained selection as "loyalty"/"trust", some descriptive detail is not in the abstract, and the body uses causal verbs the caveat disclaims.

issues.label: Headline reframes constrained choice as loyalty and opportunism as trust
issues.as_written: Why India's lowest-income shoppers stay loyal to one store — and it isn't trust
issues.abstract_says: The findings indicate that bounded rationality and lock-in significantly contribute to CRS, which, in turn, directly predicts CBS. Opportunism, although present, does not substantially influence CRS or CBS.
issues.problem: The study measures constrained retail selection (shopping at one store because of limited options), not loyalty in the attitudinal sense; and "perceived opportunism" (suspicion of exploitation) is a narrower construct than "trust".
issues.suggested_fix: Reword to e.g. "Why India's lowest-income shoppers are locked into one store — and suspicion of the retailer isn't the reason".

issues.label: Unlisted detail about what lock-in comprises
issues.as_written: lock-in — credit ties, proximity, dependence on a single shopkeeper — significantly drove constrained store selection
issues.abstract_says: consumer vulnerability activates bounded rationality, perceived opportunism, and lock-in effects, which together shape constrained retail selection (CRS) and constrained brand selection (CBS)
issues.problem: The abstract does not specify that lock-in consists of credit ties, proximity and dependence on one shopkeeper. Unverifiable from abstract only.
issues.suggested_fix: Attribute the specifics to the paper's measures or drop the parenthetical gloss.

issues.label: Causal verb for cross-sectional survey data
issues.as_written: Bounded rationality (limited information and literacy) and lock-in ... significantly drove constrained store selection, which in turn constrained which brands people could buy.
issues.abstract_says: bounded rationality and lock-in significantly contribute to CRS, which, in turn, directly predicts CBS
issues.problem: "Drove" and "constrained which brands people could buy" imply causation from a cross-sectional PLS-SEM model, which the digest's own caveat says cannot be established.
issues.suggested_fix: Use "were significantly associated with" and "which in turn predicted".

fact_check.headline: Giving your shopping assistant a face: when human-looking AI avatars actually lift engagement
fact_check.notes: Design, mediator and both moderators are reported correctly; the "Why it matters" line generalizes the abstract's "comparatively modest" label (which applies to one association in Study 2) to the overall engagement lift.

issues.label: "Modest" applied to the wrong effect
issues.as_written: this work suggests the lift is real but modest
issues.abstract_says: Study 1 shows that higher visual-form anthropomorphism increases user engagement intention, with emotional connection accounting for a meaningful but partial share of the effect. Study 2 provides associative support for the core relationships, although the association between anthropomorphism and emotional connection is comparatively modest.
issues.problem: The abstract calls the anthropomorphism–emotional connection association in Study 2 comparatively modest; it does not characterize the overall engagement-intention lift as modest. The digest's caveat gets this right, but the body sentence does not.
issues.suggested_fix: Rewrite as "the engagement lift is real, but emotional connection explains only part of it, and the anthropomorphism–emotion link was comparatively modest in the survey study".

fact_check.headline: Scams are now a marketing problem: researchers reframe AI fraud as 'malicious persuasion'
fact_check.notes: Conceptual nature, the simplicity/sophistication/scale framing, the dynamic vulnerability argument and the empowerment agenda all match; caveats correctly note no new empirical evidence.

fact_check.headline: The original purpose-driven brand: what Gandhi's homespun cloth campaign got right — and where it hit a wall
fact_check.notes: Design, sources, theoretical lenses, findings and the stated limitation on archival material all match the abstract.

sections.trends: The previous run on this topic (2026-09-30) selected no studies, so there is no study-level comparison to make. The 16 studies in this digest stand on their own as the first substantive batch since the prior cycle.
sections.feature_pitch:
**The pattern:** A striking share of this batch tests standard retail playbook moves against real operational data — and the playbook loses. Eight years of Nordic order history found the "bad returner" is mostly an artifact of tenure, not behavior ("The myth of the 'bad returner'", W7221059811); 108,566 live chatbot sessions found rule-based bots outperforming LLM bots on efficiency and effectiveness (W7214950393); minute-level Taobao data found chat engagement and sales pulling in opposite directions (W7220454801); a platform rollout found AI review summaries increasing rather than cannibalizing user reviews (W7220470690); 30 months of B2B seller data found online reputation and trade-show presence substituting for each other rather than compounding (W7220830415); and a 71-week, 24-retailer traffic panel found paid search quietly feeding the "free" direct and organic traffic that last-click models credit instead (W7220946924).

**Why pitch this now:** Retailers are simultaneously tightening returns policies, replacing scripted chatbots with generative AI, and cutting performance-marketing budgets under margin pressure — three decisions this evidence suggests are being made on untested folk wisdom rather than on their own logs.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the widening gap between what retail operators assume and what their operational data shows, built around the specific assumptions now failing audit, written for senior retail and marketing decision-makers who are setting next year's budgets. The honest framing is methodological as much as managerial: these are mostly single-firm, observational findings, so the pitch is "go measure this yourself," not "the industry is wrong."

**Potential headlines:**
- The retail playbook moves that operational data doesn't back up
- The serial returner your policy is built around may not exist
- Your 2027 retail budget is funding problems the evidence says you don't have

**Potential outlets:**
- **Retail Dive** — returns crackdowns and chatbot replacement programs are its core operational beat, and this gives both a data-backed counterargument.
- **MIT Sloan Management Review** — fits its long-running interest in the gap between managerial intuition and the firm's own measurement, and tolerates the methodological caveats.
- **Modern Retail** — covers the practical mechanics of returns, live commerce and AI customer service at the retailer level, where these findings land directly.
- **Digiday** — the paid-search halo and the engagement-versus-sales split in live streams speak straight to its attribution and measurement audience.
sections.pitch_ideas:
- **Tell shoppers they're building a collection, not just buying a thing (Work ID W7221306245):** After a decade of frictionless checkout, evidence that making the hunt harder can make shoppers want the item more — for a CMO-audience column or a consumer-psychology explainer in a general-interest outlet.
- **Launching a green product line lifted the parent brand — but only for firms with clean reputations (Work ID W7221350449):** Sustainability launches pay a brand-equity dividend that firms with weak ethical records can't collect — for a sustainability or brand-strategy feature in marketing trade press.
- **In live shopping, the host's mood moves sales — and the sidekick may be costing you money (Work ID W7220454801):** Live commerce teams are optimizing for comment volume while the assistant driving that chatter is associated with lower sales — for a marketing-trade news brief or a social-commerce explainer.
- **When the shock hit, paid search carried e-commerce revenue — and Facebook ads brought visitors who didn't buy (Work ID W7220946924):** Paid search spending today predicts tomorrow's "free" direct and organic traffic, which last-click attribution systematically hides — for a performance-marketing or media-measurement column.
- **A little blue check moved eyeballs — and choices — in a risky online marketplace (Work ID W7221510551):** A randomly assigned badge carrying zero quality information more than doubled selection rates, raising the question of what verification actually certifies — for a consumer-tech or marketplace-trust explainer in a general-interest outlet.
- **Loyalty programs don't fail on rewards alone — trust and commitment have to show up too (Work ID W7204202782):** The shopper most inclined to hunt deals extracts most of the program's value, which argues for segmenting by engagement propensity instead of adding points — for a retail CRM trade piece, with a personal-finance sidebar on whether your supermarket card is worth carrying.
- **AI review summaries didn't silence shoppers — they wrote more reviews, and better ones (Work ID W7220470690):** The feature retailers feared would kill user-generated content appears to recruit it, and shifts reviewers toward filling gaps the summary missed — for a marketing-trade news brief or a tech-and-commerce feature.
- **On B2B platforms, a strong online reputation and a strong trade-show presence cancel each other out (Work ID W7220830415):** Credibility signals substitute rather than compound, which puts top-rated sellers' event budgets under scrutiny — for a B2B marketing trade piece or an events-industry explainer.
- **Fun-seeking shoppers forgive influencers who stray off-topic; practical shoppers don't (Work ID W7221454638):** A usable matching rule for creator deals — warmth beats expertise on indulgence categories, tight domain fit is mandatory on utilitarian ones — for an influencer-marketing trade column.
- **Three in four Vietnamese grocery shoppers will pay for home delivery — but they're exquisitely sensitive to the fee (Work ID W7204970234):** Rare willingness-to-pay evidence from an emerging e-grocery market arguing flat shipping fees leave demand on the table — for a retail trade explainer or an emerging-markets business outlet.
- **The myth of the "bad returner" (Work ID W7221059811):** Returning becomes near-universal with tenure and had no detectable effect on later spending, so the profit lever is reverse-logistics cost, not customer punishment — for a retail trade feature and, separately, a consumer piece on whether returning items hurts your standing with a retailer.
- **Simple beats smart: basic rule-based chatbots outperformed LLM bots on retail service logs (Work ID W7214950393):** Live deployment logs where the scripted bot beat the generative one, and where customer effort predicted repeat use better than getting the answer right — for a customer-experience trade piece or an AI-skepticism column in business press.
- **Why India's lowest-income shoppers stay loyal to one store — and it isn't trust (Work ID W7214970397):** Credit ties and proximity settle brand choice before any brand competes, raising whether emerging-market growth reflects preference or constraint — for an emerging-markets business feature or a development-economics-adjacent general-interest piece.
- **Giving your shopping assistant a face (Work ID W7215066966):** The humanized avatar lift is real but modest and gated on perceived authenticity and tech familiarity — for a design-and-CX trade brief.
- **Scams are now a marketing problem (Work ID W7211892755):** The uncomfortable overlap between legitimate urgency and scarcity tactics and the patterns consumers are being trained to distrust — for a brand-strategy or trust-and-safety column, with a consumer angle on victimization as a cycle rather than a character flaw.
- **The original purpose-driven brand (Work ID W7214900383):** A century-old stress test showing identity-led demand outrunning the supply chain needed to serve it affordably — for a business-history essay or a purpose-branding feature.
